segments.t: Outside the community center, Gabriel confronts young actor Dylan to salvage Franck Dubosc's reputation. Desperate to make Dylan drop his complaint, Gabriel resorts to clumsy accusations until Franck steps in with a surprising discovery. Let's listen to their conversation in French first.
Dylan! Attends une seconde, s'il te plaît.
Qu'est-ce que tu veux de moi?
Franck n'a rien à voir là-dedans.
S'il te plaît, retire ta plainte.
Non, je ne retire rien du tout.
Tu files du fric à tes amis?
Pourquoi tu me cherches des histoires?
Voilà ce que je te propose.
Tu ramènes ton dealer sur le tournage?
C'est un beau stéréotype ridicule.
Vas-y, fais ce que tu veux!
Quel connard, je n'y crois pas!
Je crois que tu te trompes.
C'était son orthophoniste, pas un dealer.
Let's examine the conversation line by line and explore the French expressions.
Dylan! Attends une seconde, s'il te plaît.
'Dylan! Wait a second, please.' Gabriel tries to stop the young actor before he walks away. The reflexive pronoun sits right in front of the verb for 'wait', turning the action back onto the subject.
Qu'est-ce que tu veux de moi?
'What do you want from me?' Dylan reacts defensively to being cornered outside. The informal 'you' form around 'want' marks a direct, personal relationship.
Franck n'a rien à voir là-dedans.
'Franck has nothing to do with it.' Gabriel insists that Franck Dubosc is completely innocent in this conflict. The clause hinges on the everyday verb meaning 'has'.
S'il te plaît, retire ta plainte.

'Please, withdraw your complaint.' Notice how the short vowel drops before a vowel sound around 'withdraw', making the phrase flow smoothly as one unit. Notice how the short vowel drops before a vowel sound around 'withdraw', making the phrase flow smoothly as one unit.
Non, je ne retire rien du tout.
'No, I am withdrawing nothing at all.' Dylan firmly refuses to drop the charges against Franck. The two-part French negation brackets the verb for 'withdraw' on both sides.
Tu files du fric à tes amis?

'Do you hand out cash to your friends?' Gabriel probes Dylan about the money he just handed over. In everyday spoken French, rising intonation on 'hand over' at the end is enough to turn the sentence into a question.
Pourquoi tu me cherches des histoires?

'Why are you picking fights with me?' Dylan challenges Gabriel's hostile and intrusive questions. The reflexive pronoun sits right in front of the verb for 'seek', turning the action back onto the subject.
Voilà ce que je te propose.
'Here is what I offer you.' Gabriel attempts to lay down an ultimatum to settle the issue. The clause hinges on the everyday verb meaning 'propose'.
Tu ramènes ton dealer sur le tournage?

'Are you bringing your dealer on set?' Gabriel recklessly accuses Dylan of illegal drug dealings. The verb meaning 'bring along' pairs naturally with the noun for 'drug dealer' in everyday conversation.
C'est un beau stéréotype ridicule.
'That is a nice ridiculous stereotype.' Dylan points out the insulting bias behind Gabriel's accusation. The key noun here means 'stereotype', anchored by its matching French article.
Vas-y, fais ce que tu veux!
'Go ahead, do what you want!' Dylan dismisses Gabriel and dares him to carry out his threat. Dylan uses the casual singular 'you' with 'do', showing close familiarity.
Quel connard, je n'y crois pas!
'What an idiot, I do not believe it!' Gabriel vents his irritation once Dylan turns his back. The verb meaning 'believe' pairs naturally with the noun for 'jerk' in everyday conversation.
Je crois que tu te trompes.

'I think you are mistaken.' Franck Dubosc steps in to correct Gabriel's hasty conclusion. The reflexive pronoun sits right in front of the verb for 'believe', turning the action back onto the subject.
C'était son orthophoniste, pas un dealer.

'It was his speech therapist, not a dealer.' Franck clarifies the true identity of the man Dylan met. Notice how 'was' leads directly into the noun meaning 'speech therapist'. Now let's listen to the complete discussion once more to reinforce the vocabulary.

Gabriel tries every trick to protect his client, even making baseless accusations against Dylan. When you watch the episode, listen out for the expressions meaning 'wait' and 'second'. You'll catch them now. See you next time.
